Art & Culture.title: Lucien Smith’s Last Paintings Brought His Artistry ‘Full Circle’
Art & Culture.text: SummaryLucien Smith's final works are currently being shown at Tripoli Gallery in 'Delay of Game,' now on view until November 23The exhibition features four large-scale 'Rain Paintings' created this past August as part of a performance pieceThe works trace back to the early-career series that initially put Smith on the map Lucien Smith spent August at an abandoned baseball field in Montauk, New York, creating what would be his final exhibition. It was Rain Paintings, canvases sprayed by paint-filled fire extinguishers, that launched Smith, an artist turned Serving the People founder and FOOD revivalist, into stardom. Completed just a month prior to his death, at 37, last month, he saw the new show, Delay of Game, as a return to his early-career practice.Tripoli Gallery in Wainscott, New York, is currently presenting Smith’s final paintings in its ongoing exhibition. The show, which was originally slated for September and rescheduled in lieu of his death, features four large-scale Rain Paintings created as part of a live performance. Its title is drawn from a baseball call: when rain stops the play, the grounds crew roll out a tarp to protect the field. For Smith, the tarp catches the paint.Canvases take up dedicated walls, their fields of green and pink speckles have an effervescent, meditative quality, reflecting Smith’s own introspection and acceptance at the time of their creation. “A process like this is a gift,” he said. “When I was younger I thought I needed to keep looking, that landing on one thing so early meant I’d be missing something. I let the market and outside criticism dictate my practice, and that was a mistake. Life has taken me full circle. I think it is time to return to the process I was given.”Delay of Game is now on view until November 23.Tripoli Gallery26 Ardsley Road,Wainscott, NY 11975Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: 'Godzilla Minus One' Is One of the Most Important Blockbusters in Years and Nobody Is Talking About It Enough
Entertainment.text: The kaiju genre has never really been about the monster. That’s the thing most Western attempts at Godzilla have fundamentally misread, loading the films with destruction tourism and treating the human characters as connective tissue between set-pieces rather than the actual point of the whole exercise. Takashi Yamazaki understood something that Roland Emmerich and even Gareth Edwards only partially grasped: Godzilla works when the monster means something, and Godzilla Minus One built its entire architecture around that idea with a precision that very few blockbusters of any budget have managed in recent memory.The setup is postwar Japan, 1945. The country is already in ruins, already processing an incomprehensible level of collective loss, and then Godzilla arrives. The film’s title refers to that compounding of disaster, a nation that was already at zero being pushed into negative numbers by something it has no framework to understand or resist. It is an elegant and genuinely devastating premise, and Yamazaki uses it not as backdrop but as the emotional engine the whole film runs on.Ryunosuke Kamiki plays Koichi Shikishima, a former kamikaze pilot who survived the war carrying guilt he doesn’t know how to put down. The film is really about that guilt, about what it means to have lived when others didn’t and what it takes to find a reason to keep going, and Kamiki carries it in a way that makes every Godzilla encounter feel personal rather than spectacle. By the time the film reaches its climax, you are not watching humans try to defeat a monster. You are watching a man decide whether his life is worth something, and the monster is just the thing forcing the question.The visual effects won the Academy Award and deserved it, which almost undersells the achievement. Godzilla Minus One was made on a budget of roughly fifteen million dollars, a figure that makes the quality of what appears on screen genuinely difficult to process. The atomic breath sequence in Ginza is as viscerally terrifying as anything the genre has produced, and the film’s restraint around Godzilla’s appearances, keeping him scarce enough that his presence never normalizes, is the kind of discipline that most studios with ten times the budget don’t have the confidence to exercise.What Yamazaki pulled off is the thing that makes the original 1954 Gojira so enduring and so rarely replicated: he made a monster movie where the monster is a metaphor that actually holds weight. Godzilla here is the war continuing by other means, the destruction that doesn’t stop just because the fighting did, the trauma that outlasts the event that caused it. That reading is built into the film’s bones rather than imposed on it by critics looking for something to say.Most blockbusters ask you to be impressed. Godzilla Minus One asks you to feel something, and then earns the right to ask.Supergirl is available now on Cathay Pacific‘s award-winning inflight entertainment system.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: BAO Brings BFF and Its Taiwanese Fried Chicken to Singapore
Entertainment.text: SummaryBAO’s BFF pop-up lands at Singapore’s New Bahru from November 11 through December 28.The Chicken Chopper headlines a Taiwanese fast-food-inspired menu.Craft teas, grab-and-go snacks and convenience-store culture complete the concept.After making its homecoming debut in Taiwan earlier this year, BFF (BAO Fast Foods) is taking its next step in Singapore with a seven-week pop-up at New Bahru from November 11 through December 28, 2026.Developed by London restaurant group BAO with Singapore’s The Lo & Behold Group, BFF reimagines the fast-food format through the lens of Taiwanese convenience-store and street-food culture, treating speed and accessibility as only part of the experience. The Singapore edition will function as a testing ground as the team continues developing BFF ahead of its first permanent location, planned for the first half of 2027.Beyond the kitchen, the New Bahru space will borrow from the rhythms of an Asian convenience store, combining grab-and-go stations with Taiwanese snacks, Asian pantry staples, BAO-branded goods and rotating collaborations, while new items will be introduced throughout the run.At the center of the menu is the Chicken Chopper, BFF’s take on Taiwanese fried chicken and a recipe that has reportedly gone through more than 140 iterations. The bone is deliberately left attached as a handle before the chicken is dipped in soymilk batter and tapioca starch for a thin, crackly crust, then finished in three ways: Original Crispy with Taiwanese white pepper; Flame Glazed, brushed with either soy-garlic glaze or mala hot honey before being torched; and Master Scalded, dipped into a hot master sauce infused with soy, star anise and cinnamon. It can be ordered as a ricebox or combo, alongside dishes such as Dan Dan Noodles and a Beef Cup Noodle topped with meat carved from a slow-roasting spit.Drinks similarly sidestep standard fast-food conventions with Taiwanese craft teas developed with S.C Labs, including nitro-brewed Alishan Wintermelon and carbonated Orange Guava Beauty Tea, while an OATSIDE collaboration brings a peanut oat milk drink with boba and tea jelly. Egg sandos, marinated eggs, “Fried Rice” quinoa, golden kimchi, broth and soy puddings round out the grab-and-go selection. The pop-up will operate from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., Wednesday through Monday, with 9 p.m. last orders, and will be walk-in only. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BFF | Fast Food Convienence Store (@baofastfoods)Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Dream Golf Trip Through the Canadian Rockies
Entertainment.text: There are golf trips you come home from needing another vacation. You know, the kinds where you're stacking rounds back-to-back and spending car rides with roller bags on your lap. But over six nights in the Canadian Rockies this September, recovery and relaxation was given as much consideration as the rounds themselves.Fairmont hosted our group across three of its mountain properties: Fairmont Banff Springs, Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise and Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge. Golf was a big part of the itinerary, with rounds at two Stanley Thompson designs. Around those rounds were forest bathing, hiking, thermal bathing and enough time outdoors to make the distinction between activity and relaxation feel less obvious.The trip introduced us to Fairmont’s Wellness Without Walls campaign, which launched earlier this year with Kylian Mbappé as the brand’s first Wellness Ambassador. Across these three properties, the idea had a clear proposition: make it easier for guests to stay active, recover and spend time in their surroundings.Through its partnership with Hyperice, Fairmont offers access to recovery tools including Normatec compression boots, a Hypervolt massage gun and a Venom heated vibration wrap for the back. The Nike gear lending program addresses a simpler obstacle: arriving somewhere with the intention of exercising and realizing you haven’t packed for it. Shoes and workout clothing can be borrowed during a stay.These are useful things to have available when you travel, particularly if you want to keep your luggage manageable. Over the week, though, the strongest expression of the wellness proposition came from the places themselves.Banff: Golf Beneath the PeaksFairmont Banff Springs makes an impression before you have done very much at all. The castle-like hotel has a European grandeur, with stone corridors, period details and a scale that makes getting slightly lost feel like part of the stay. It is rugged and imposing from outside; inside, there always seems to be another staircase or room to discover.Down at the golf course, the mountains present their own architectural presence. On the Stanley Thompson 18, they sit so close to your sight lines that it can be difficult to separate the hole in front of you from everything rising behind it. There is the shot you need to hit, and then there is the view competing for your attention.We played the 18-hole course as well as the separate Tunnel Mountain 9, seeing Banff in both moody early-fall weather and clear sunshine. Under clouds, the landscape felt enclosed and atmospheric. When the sky opened, the surrounding peaks came into view with a clarity that changed our sense of the place.The schedule gave us reasons to look beyond the golf, too. A guided forest-bathing walk with a certified guide on the resort’s activities team offered another way to spend time in the same landscape. Meals reconvened the group, while a Hyperice recovery lounge at the clubhouse connected the performance element of the trip directly to our time on the course.Lake Louise: Step OutsideAt Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise, the relationship between the hotel and the landscape is even more connected. The hotel sits directly on Lake Louise, within Banff National Park and the wider Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks UNESCO World Heritage Site. The familiar postcard is right there: turquoise water, steep mountain walls and the Victoria Glacier beyond. Seeing it from the hotel, then walking outside and finding yourself at the edge of it, is another experience entirely. The color of the lake is difficult to appreciate fully through a screen.That convenience defined our stay. One morning, we stepped out for a roughly four-hour guided hike, swapping the busy lakeshore for trails and elevated views. Later, we took canoes across the lake toward the hotel. Over the course of a day, the same scene could be something you looked out at, walked through and paddled across.Lake Louise has no golf course. It did, however, offer the most concentrated recovery experience of the trip. BASIN Glacial Waters, which opened in September 2025, adds an indoor-outdoor thermal bathing destination to a hotel that already has a treatment-based spa. Having both initially sounds extravagant. Once inside, the distinction becomes clear: BASIN is organized around heat, cold, water and rest, with the lake and mountains remaining part of the experience.Our first visit followed the golf at Banff, with a guided recovery sequence. The next afternoon, we returned for a longer session, including a private two-hour window in which our group could photograph and film the facilities before the usual no-tech policy resumed. The setting makes it easy to linger. Between a morning on the trail and an afternoon moving through the thermal experience, a day without golf felt fully occupied without becoming overloaded.The Road to JasperThe journey north to Jasper deserves plenty of time to savor it. The Icefields Parkway runs through a landscape that keeps offering reasons to stop. We had a clear day for the drive and broke it up with an icefield, a waterfall, a lake and a lookout. There were far more potential stops than we could reasonably make. Even the stretches between them demanded attention. For much of the route, phone service disappeared. With so much outside the window, there was little reason to miss it.Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge offered another change of pace. A central Main Lodge anchors the property, with cabins and other accommodations spread around Lac Beauvert. After the scale of Banff Springs and the constant activity around Lake Louise, Jasper felt more spacious. The mountains were still there, but they seemed to step back a little, and arriving felt like an exhale.Its golf course rewarded that extra space in the itinerary. Another Stanley Thompson design, Jasper Park Lodge Golf Club was impressive on the first round and more interesting on the second. There is enough subtlety in the routing and the decisions it asks of you that familiarity becomes valuable quickly. Seeing a hole once gives you a better sense of how you might want to play it next time.We had the benefit of local professional insight into the course’s history and strategy. Our first round included associate golf professional Nick Armour, whose perspective added context to what we were seeing. By the end of the second round, we had a fuller appreciation of the course and were glad to have had the chance to return.The aftermath of the 2024 wildfire was also part of our experience of Jasper. Its effects were visible, giving the stay a context beyond the scenery and hospitality. Alongside those reminders, we encountered a destination continuing to welcome people back. A free afternoon left room to choose how much more activity we wanted: hiking, a bike ride, or a glacial plunge and sauna. By then, the freedom to decide felt as valuable as any particular amenity.Across six nights, the trip immersed us in three different versions of the Rockies: Banff’s time capsule, Lake Louise’s grandeur and Jasper’s room to breathe. Although golf gave us a familiar way into the landscape, hiking and recovery time gave us a way to truly relax into it.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Science & Technology.title: Rethinking Modern Workspace Lighting: The Design and Science Behind BenQ ScreenBar
Science & Technology.text: For design lovers and digital creators, a desk is rarely just a place to park a laptop. It’s a carefully curated studio space where every detail, from a custom mechanical keyboard and monitor arm to a thoughtfully chosen desk mat, serves a purpose. But one essential element has often been overlooked: lighting designed around the way people use screens. As screens became central to how we work, create, and connect, desk lighting has not always kept pace with the needs of a screen-centered workspace. BenQ set out to rethink workspace lighting as an essential part of the digital ecosystem, bringing together human-centered design and optical expertise to create a lighting experience purpose-built for the digital workspace.BenQ’s approach to desk lighting extends beyond a one-size-fits-all solution. From the ScreenBar® models designed for a wide range of monitors to the iScreenBar, designed to complement the iMac’s distinctive silhouette, to the ScreenBar Max, developed for dual-monitor setups, each product reflects a considered approach to industrial design and the needs of different workspaces. Every curve, finish, and material choice is made to respect the underlying hardware. As JC Pan, Head of the Digital Lifestyle Product Business Unit at BenQ, explains: “The initial mounting concept proved workable, so subsequent iterations focused on refining it rather than replacing it with a different approach. The main challenge was to integrate iScreenBar with the iMac’s silhouette while maintaining microphone clearance and a secure mount.” That hyper-fixation on detail went so far as using acoustic frequency-response measurements to design mount cutouts that wouldn’t muffle the iMac’s internal microphones, paired with hidden magnetic cable organizers to keep Apple’s iconic logo completely unobstructed.Beyond Brightness: Lighting for Visual ComfortBeyond pure aesthetics, BenQ approaches desktop illumination as a way to support visual comfort for long-haul creators. After an eight-hour editing session, screen brightness may not be the only factor contributing to visual discomfort; strong lighting contrast between a glowing display and a dark room can also play a role. By pairing full-spectrum LEDs with precise color temperature control, creators can shift seamlessly from energizing cool light, up to 6500K on iScreenBar, for example, during daytime brainstorms to a warm, relaxing 2700K setting during midnight sessions. On dual-monitor setups, ScreenBar Max takes ambient balance even further by illuminating the wall behind the screens, drastically softening the harsh contrast between bright displays and their background.The Unique Optical Engineering: ASYM-Light™The optical engineering driving this experience is equal parts math and physics. “The core of BenQ’s ASYM-Light™ technology is an exclusive, eight-segment curved reflector,” says Pan. “BenQ simulates millions of light paths to determine the optimal combination of curves, shaping each beam to illuminate the work surface with minimal spill.” Made from pure-silver coated PVD aluminum with over 98% reflectivity, this precision mirror system bends light downward onto the desk while light-absorbing outlets catch any remaining stray rays, ensuring zero glare hits the glass or the user’s eyes.From User Insights to Continuous InnovationBehind ScreenBar is a deeper foundation of optical research and user-centered innovation, developed through BenQ’s Smart Lighting Lab. While traditional lighting design assumed brighter desks equaled better visibility, real-world testing with heavy screen users revealed the exact opposite. As Pan recalls: “As early as 2015, through in-depth interviews with heavy screen users, we discovered a counterintuitive insight: many creators preferred working in extremely dim or completely dark environments to maintain a sense of immersion. During early prototype testing, creators’ unexpected complaint was not that the lighting was insufficient, but that ‘too much light actually disrupted the visual depth and contrast of the screen.’”That key realization fundamentally altered BenQ’s approach: the goal wasn’t to flood a room with lumens, but to deliver exact, controlled light precisely where reading and writing happen while preserving screen contrast. That thinking takes different forms in different workspaces: iScreenBar complements the iMac’s design, while ScreenBar Max’s ASYM-TriZone Light™ redistributes light to address the coverage challenges of dual-monitor setups. Though designed for different setups, both reflect the same philosophy: understand how people work, then shape the lighting around their needs. As Pan puts it, “great lighting is not about making everything brighter but about delivering the right light to the right place.”Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Lysosomes are the final destination of damaged or unwanted proteins and structures flagged for destruction by the cellular maintenance processes of autophagy. Lysosomes are known to become dysfunctional with age, for reasons that are not fully explored.
